titleText.es: Ah, tu hermano es Luke. Lo siento, deberías haberlo mencionado antes.
titleText.en: Oh, your brother is Luke.  Sorry, should've mentioned that first.
titleText.noteEn: The title text supplies a final version of the recurring joke: Han should have disclosed the sibling relationship before making the preceding remarks. The Spanish raster deliberately localizes several ad-libs rather than copying the official English text word for word; for example, its asteroid odds are 9721 to 1 instead of 3720 to 1, and it renders the playful reaction ‘Wowzers’ as fantabuloso.

regions.labelEs: HARRISON FORD IMPROVISÓ SU CÉLEBRE FRASE "LO SÉ" EN EL IMPERIO CONTRAATACA. AQUÍ SE MUESTRAN OTROS DE SUS IMPROMPTUS MENOS EXITOSOS:

excludedUnits.rationale: Harrison is an unchanged personal name rather than a Spanish lexical word.
Ford is an unchanged surname rather than a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Célebre has one singular form for both genders, so it matches the feminine singular noun frase without changing.
Lo stands for the thing known and appears immediately before the finite verb sé.
Se presents the impromptus as the things being shown, while the person showing them is not named.
Impromptus names the items first; menos adjusts the degree of the following descriptive adjective exitosos.
Exitosos uses masculine plural -os to match the plural noun impromptus; menos stays unchanged.

regions.labelEs: TE QUIERO.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the person receiving the affection and comes before the finite verb quiero.

regions.labelEs: ¿ME LO DICES O ME LO CUENTAS?

applications.explanationEn: Lo stands for the thing being said and appears before the finite verb dices.
Lo stands for the information being recounted and appears before the finite verb cuentas.

applications.exampleEs: ME LO DICES O ME LO CUENTAS
applications.explanationEn: The entire seven-word question is the colloquial formula here, signaling already-familiar information rather than asking a literal either-or question.

regions.labelEs: ¡SEÑOR, LA PROBABILIDAD DE NAVEGAR CON ÉXITO A TRAVÉS DE UN CAMPO DE ASTEROIDES ES APROXIMADAMENTE DE 9721 A 1!

excludedUnits.rationale: This digit sequence is the first quantity in the stated odds, not a Spanish lexical word.
This digit is the second quantity in the stated odds, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Probabilidad names the chance, de links it to the action, and navegar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Con éxito follows navegar and characterizes the action as successful.

applications.exampleEs: A TRAVÉS DE UN CAMPO DE ASTEROIDES
applications.explanationEn: A través de forms the through/across expression, and the remaining words name the area being traversed.
De marks the first quantity in the odds and a introduces the second; the digit labels themselves are kept as numeric exclusions.

regions.labelEs: ¿EN SERIO? ... DIOS.

applications.explanationEn: En and serio form the fixed reaction that asks whether the information is genuine.

regions.labelEs: TE QUIERO.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the person receiving the affection and comes before the finite verb quiero.

regions.labelEs: ¡OH! EH, ESO EXPLICA EL BESO DE ANTES.

applications.explanationEn: De antes marks the kiss as the earlier one rather than a new event.

regions.labelEs: TE QUIERO.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the person receiving the affection and comes before the finite verb quiero.

regions.labelEs: ME ESTOY TIRANDO A TU HERMANO.

applications.explanationEn: Me marks the pronominal verb, estoy is the changing helper, and tirando supplies the ongoing action.

applications.exampleEs: ME ESTOY TIRANDO A TU HERMANO
applications.explanationEn: Me and tirando form the informal pronominal expression, estoy makes it ongoing, and a introduces the person involved.
A introduces the specific person who is the object, and tu hermano identifies him.

regions.labelEs: LAS RELIGIONES Y LAS ARMAS ANTIGUAS NO VALEN NADA COMPARADAS CON LAS TIJERAS, AUNQUE SÍ VENCEN AL PAPEL Y A LA PIEDRA.

applications.explanationEn: Armas names the things first, and the neutral descriptive adjective antiguas follows it.
Antiguas uses feminine plural -as to match the feminine plural noun armas.

applications.exampleEs: NO VALEN NADA COMPARADAS CON LAS TIJERAS
applications.explanationEn: No, valen, and nada reject the value of the earlier plural items; comparadas agrees with those feminine plural items, and con introduces the comparison reference.
Accented sí emphasizes that the action expressed by vencen really does happen despite the preceding negative comparison.

applications.exampleEs: VENCEN AL PAPEL Y A LA PIEDRA
applications.explanationEn: Vencen governs both coordinated opponents: al combines a with el before papel, while a stays separate before la piedra.

regions.labelEs: TE QUIERO.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the person receiving the affection and comes before the finite verb quiero.

regions.labelEs: PERFECTO. OYE, ESTA COSA ESTÁ MUY, MUY FRÍA.

applications.explanationEn: Oye is the irregular positive tú command used here to get one familiar listener's attention.
Está carries the present state, and fría describes that state; the intervening muy words intensify it.
Fría uses feminine singular -a to match the feminine singular noun cosa.

regions.labelEs: TE QUIERO.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the person receiving the affection and comes before the finite verb quiero.

regions.labelEs: FANTABULOSO.
GENERAL SOLO, ¿ESTÁ LISTO SU EQUIPO DE ASALTO?

excludedUnits.rationale: Solo is the unchanged fictional surname in the title General Solo, not the Spanish adjective or adverb solo.

applications.explanationEn: Está carries the current state, and listo identifies that state as ready.
Listo uses masculine singular -o because the thing described is the masculine singular noun equipo.

regions.labelEs: A DURAS PENAS.

applications.explanationEn: All three words form the fixed expression for managing something only with difficulty or barely.

regions.labelEs: ESTÁN BASTANTE BORRACHOS.

applications.explanationEn: Están carries the group's current state, borrachos names that state, and bastante strengthens the description.

regions.labelEs: ANTES BESARÍA A UN WOOKIE.

excludedUnits.rationale: Wookie is the unchanged fictional species name, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Antes makes the would-form besaría express the option the speaker would choose sooner; the rejected alternative is supplied by the scene.
Besaría keeps the full verb besar and adds -ía to express what the speaker would do.
A marks the sentient, person-like creature as the object of the kissing action; the fictional species name itself remains an audited exclusion.

regions.labelEs: VAYA, YO TAMBIÉN, PERO CHEWIE NUNCA PARECE INTERESADO.

excludedUnits.rationale: Chewie is the unchanged fictional character name, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Yo changes the person to the speaker and también affirms the same preference just expressed; the repeated action is understood and omitted.
Parece reports an impression, and interesado names the apparent state while agreeing with the masculine character.

regions.labelEs: QUIZÁS DEBERÍA DEJARME CRECER EL PELO.

applications.explanationEn: Debería presents the action as a tentative idea or piece of self-advice, while dejar remains in its unchanged form inside dejarme.
Me attaches directly to the unchanged verb dejar and identifies the speaker as the person whose appearance is involved.
Dejarme identifies the speaker, crecer names the growth, and el pelo supplies the body feature being allowed to grow longer.

cards.answerEn: improvised; made up on the spot
cards.noteEn: Improvisó is the completed-past form of improvisar for one person or thing.

cards.promptEs: «Lo sé» · El Imperio contraataca · respuestas improvisadas
cards.answerEn: The comic replaces Han Solo's famous improvised reply to Leia with a series of deliberately worse ad-libs across scenes from the original Star Wars trilogy.
cards.noteEn: In The Empire Strikes Back, Harrison Ford famously replied “I know” to Leia's declaration of love instead of the scripted response. The comic tests absurd alternatives in that carbon-freezing scene, then carries the same premise into the asteroid field, lightsaber training, a Rebel briefing, and the Hoth tunnel. Knowledge of those recurring characters and scenes explains why the mismatched lines are funny.
Su agrees with the possessed thing, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can mean his, her, its, their, or formal your; the surrounding context identifies the owner.
Célebre has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: For dialogue in a film or play, frase can refer to a spoken line.

example.es: Recuerdo una frase de la película.
example.en: I remember a line from the movie.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.
Imperio is a masculine noun, so a particular empire normally takes the article el.
Contraataca is the present form of contraatacar for one person or thing.

cards.answerEn: marks an action whose doer is not named
cards.noteEn: Before a third-person verb, se can focus on what happens rather than who does it. English often uses a passive form such as ‘is requested’ or ‘have been discovered.’

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona (sin nombrar quién actúa)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish focus on an action or result without naming who does it?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person verb and state what happens; the person doing it can remain unnamed.
cards.noteEn: English often uses a passive form. Spanish may use se with a simple verb or with a completed construction such as se han encontrado. Other uses of se follow different patterns.
Sus can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or formal “your.” It agrees with the plural things possessed, not with the owner; context tells you whose they are.

example.es: El jefe llamó a sus empleados.

cards.noteEn: An impromptu is something said or done without preparation. Its plural is impromptus.

example.en: His improvised remarks surprised the audience.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.
Exitosos describes several masculine or mixed-gender things.

cards.answerEn: I love; I care deeply for (a person)
cards.noteEn: Querer usually means “to want,” but when its object is a person it commonly expresses affection or love. Te quiero is often less intense than te amo, though usage varies.

example.en: I love you very much, Grandma.

cards.promptEs: ¿me lo dices o me lo cuentas?
cards.questionEn: What colloquial expression says that you already know or have experienced what someone has just told you?
cards.answerEn: Use ¿me lo dices o me lo cuentas? It works like ‘tell me about it’ and can sound ironic or slightly brusque.
cards.noteEn: Although decir and contar can both mean ‘to tell,’ this fixed question does not ask the listener to choose between them. It signals that the information is already familiar to the speaker; tone can also add disbelief or irritation.

example.es: —Los lunes son agotadores. —¿Me lo dices o me lo cuentas?

cards.noteEn: Contar can mean to count, but it also means to tell or recount information or a story. Cuentas is the present form for tú.

example.en: Will you tell me what happened?

cards.promptEs: probabilidad de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you name the chance of an action happening?
cards.answerEn: Use probabilidad de followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The action ends in -ar, -er, or -ir: probabilidad de ganar, de perder, or de salir. When a full clause with its own stated subject follows, Spanish commonly uses probabilidad de que plus a special possibility form instead.

example.en: There is little chance of rain.

cards.answerEn: of; links probabilidad to the possible action
cards.noteEn: After probabilidad, de can introduce an action in its unchanged dictionary form: la probabilidad de ganar.

example.es: La probabilidad de llegar a tiempo es baja.
example.en: The chance of arriving on time is low.

cards.noteEn: Navegar can describe guiding a vessel through a route or difficult area, not only traveling by boat.

example.es: Es difícil navegar por este canal.
example.en: It is difficult to navigate this channel.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens successfully?
cards.answerEn: Use con éxito after the action.
cards.noteEn: Éxito means success. Together with con, the fixed phrase describes a successful outcome, much like the English word “successfully.” It does not change for person or time.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; part of a través de (“through”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something goes or can be seen through something?
cards.answerEn: Use a través de before the thing: it means “through” or “across.”
cards.noteEn: Keep all three parts together. Before masculine singular el, de and el combine as del: a través del bosque. Before a feminine noun, use a través de la, as in a través de la ventana. The expression can describe literal passage or a figurative means.

example.es: La luz entra a través de la ventana.
example.en: The light comes in through the window.

cards.answerEn: part of a través de, “through” or “across”
no separate English word; completes a través de, “through”
no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”
Asteroide is masculine; its plural is asteroides.
Aproximadamente signals that a number or amount is not exact.

example.en: It will take approximately one hour.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a ratio stated with de ... a ...
cards.noteEn: Spanish can frame odds or a ratio with de before the first quantity and a before the second.

example.es: Las probabilidades son de dos a uno.
example.en: The odds are two to one.

cards.promptEs: de + primera cantidad + a + segunda cantidad
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish state odds or a ratio between two quantities?
cards.answerEn: Put de before the first quantity and a before the second.
cards.noteEn: This frame is common with proporción or probabilidades: de tres a uno. The numbers may use digits or number words.

example.es: Las probabilidades son de cinco a dos.
example.en: The odds are five to two.

cards.answerEn: to (between the two quantities in a ratio)
cards.noteEn: In a ratio stated as de X a Y, a introduces the second quantity.

example.es: La proporción es de tres a uno.
example.en: The ratio is three to one.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en serio (“seriously”)

cards.questionEn: How do you ask whether someone is really serious or whether something is actually true?
cards.answerEn: Use en serio to mean “seriously,” “really,” or “for real.”
cards.noteEn: En serio is a fixed expression. In a question, ¿En serio? often reacts with surprise or disbelief; in a statement, it can contrast sincerity with joking.

example.en: Are you really going to run tomorrow?

cards.noteEn: Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’
Explica is the present form of explicar for one person or thing. With a thing as its subject, it says that the thing provides the explanation.
El beso is the noun. The same spelling beso without an article can also be the verb form meaning “I kiss.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; links something to an earlier time
cards.noteEn: De antes describes something as being from before or earlier.

cards.questionEn: How can you describe something as the earlier or previous one?
cards.answerEn: Put de antes after the thing.
cards.noteEn: Depending on context, de antes can mean from before, earlier, or the previous version. It contrasts that thing with what exists now.

example.es: Me gustaba más el menú de antes.
example.en: I liked the old menu better.

cards.noteEn: Used by itself, antes can point back to an earlier time rather than introducing a following event.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.promptEs: tirarse a alguien · uso sexual informal
cards.questionEn: What informal expression says that someone is having sex with another person?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching pronominal form of tirarse, then a before the other person.
cards.noteEn: This is an informal and potentially crude sexual meaning, distinct from the ordinary meanings of tirar such as to throw or pull. The short marker changes with the subject: me tiro, te tiras, se tira, and so on.

example.es: El rumor decía que se tiraba a un compañero.
example.en: The rumor said that he was sleeping with a colleague.

cards.answerEn: sleeping with; having sex with (informal, as part of tirarse a alguien)
cards.noteEn: Tirar normally means to throw or pull. The pronominal expression tirarse a alguien is informal and means to have sex with that person; tirando is its -ando ongoing-action form.

example.es: La novela insinúa que se estaba tirando a su vecino.
example.en: The novel hints that he was sleeping with his neighbor.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general feminine plural group
cards.noteEn: Spanish often keeps las before a category discussed in general, where English may use a bare plural: las bicicletas, las herramientas.
Religión is feminine; its plural is religiones.
Arma is feminine, but singular el arma uses el because arma begins with a stressed a sound. The plural returns to las armas.
Antiguas describes more than one feminine noun.

cards.promptEs: no valer nada comparado/a/os/as con + referencia
cards.questionEn: How can you say that something does not measure up at all beside something else?
cards.answerEn: Use no, the matching form of valer, nada, a matching form of comparado, and con before the reference.
cards.noteEn: Comparado changes to comparada, comparados, or comparadas to match what is being judged. Con introduces the thing used as the standard of comparison.

example.es: Estos bocetos no valen nada comparados con el cuadro final.
example.en: These sketches are nothing compared with the final painting.

cards.noteEn: Valer can describe value or adequacy. In no valer nada comparado con, it says that one thing does not measure up at all beside another.

example.es: Estas copias no valen nada comparadas con el original.
example.en: These copies are nothing compared with the original.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.
Comparadas matches a feminine plural subject. Con introduces the reference used for comparison.

example.es: Son pequeñas comparadas con las otras.
example.en: They are small compared with the others.

cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses the plural las tijeras for one pair of scissors.
Before a verb, stressed sí can contradict a negative idea and emphasize that the action really does happen. It keeps its written accent.

example.es: No corro mucho, pero sí camino cada día.
example.en: I do not run much, but I do walk every day.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish emphasize that an action really does happen after a contrast or denial?
cards.answerEn: Put accented sí directly before the verb.
cards.noteEn: This sí is affirmative emphasis, not the unaccented condition word si. English often conveys it with stressed do or does: no canta mucho, pero sí baila.

example.en: He does not cook, although he does help.

cards.noteEn: Vencen is the present form of vencer for a plural subject. The opponent follows a.

cards.questionEn: How do you name the opponent that someone or something beats?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of vencer, then a before the opponent.
cards.noteEn: A combines with el to become al: venció al campeón. It stays separate before la, los, or las.

example.es: El equipo venció a sus rivales.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; a + el before the opponent of vencer
cards.noteEn: Vencer normally takes a before the person or thing defeated. Al combines that a with el.
Papel is masculine. In the game piedra, papel o tijeras, it names the paper option.

example.es: Elegí papel en la primera ronda.
example.en: I chose paper in the first round.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces the opponent of vencer
cards.noteEn: Use vencer a before the person or thing defeated.
Piedra is feminine. In piedra, papel o tijeras, it names the rock option.

example.es: La piedra vence a las tijeras.

cards.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: estar + palabra que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe how someone or something is feeling or doing at a particular time?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by a describing word for the state.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to match who or what has the state: estoy means “I am,” está means “he, she, or it is,” and están means “they are.” The describing word matches the person or thing in gender and number: enfadado, enfadada, enfadados, or enfadadas. This pattern presents the quality as a condition or state; ser is normally used for identity or a defining description.
Fría describes one feminine person or thing and carries a written accent on í.
Fantabuloso is a playful blend shaped like fantástico plus fabuloso rather than a standard neutral word. It can convey exaggerated enthusiasm or delight.

example.en: He described the party as fantabulous.

cards.noteEn: With estar, listo commonly means ready. It matches a masculine singular subject.

cards.answerEn: your (formal or plural, before one thing)

cards.noteEn: Equipo can also mean equipment; here it names a group of people working together.

example.en: The team is looking for a solution.

cards.noteEn: In equipo de asalto, asalto classifies the team as one assembled for an attack or strike.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a duras penas, “barely”
cards.noteEn: A is not translated separately inside the fixed expression a duras penas.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens only with great difficulty or barely happens?
cards.noteEn: The expression functions as one unit. It can describe barely managing an action or doing it with considerable effort.

example.es: A duras penas terminó la carrera.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a duras penas, “barely”
cards.noteEn: Duras is not translated separately inside the fixed expression a duras penas.

example.es: A duras penas llegó a tiempo.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a duras penas, “barely”
cards.noteEn: Penas literally relates to troubles or suffering, but the whole fixed expression a duras penas means with great difficulty or barely.

cards.answerEn: they are (in a place or state)

cards.noteEn: Before a describing word, bastante increases its degree and often means ‘quite,’ ‘fairly,’ or ‘pretty.’ It stays unchanged even when the following description changes for gender or number: bastante claro, bastante clara, bastante claros. This differs from bastante meaning ‘enough.’
Borrachos describes several men or a mixed group.
Before a would-form such as besaría, antes can mean that the speaker would sooner choose that option.

example.es: Antes caminaría que tomar ese autobús.
example.en: I would rather walk than take that bus.

cards.promptEs: antes + verbo en forma de “haría” · preferencia
cards.questionEn: How can you say that you would sooner choose one option?
cards.answerEn: Put antes before a would-form such as iría, haría, or besaría.
cards.noteEn: In this use, antes expresses preference rather than simply earlier time. A comparison with que may follow, but it can be left unstated when the rejected alternative is clear.

example.es: Antes dormiría en el suelo que volver allí.
example.en: I would rather sleep on the floor than go back there.

cards.answerEn: I would kiss; he or she would kiss
cards.noteEn: Besaría is the would-form of besar. The surrounding context identifies its subject.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person-denoting object
cards.noteEn: The personal a also appears before words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) when they directly receive an action, even though they do not identify one specific individual.
Used on its own as an exclamation, vaya can express surprise, admiration, or annoyance. This conversational use is distinct from vaya as a form of the verb ir, 'to go.'

cards.promptEs: primera afirmación; segunda persona, cosa o valor con palabras repetidas omitidas
cards.questionEn: Can Spanish leave out repeated words in the second part of a comparison or list?
cards.answerEn: Yes. State the full first part, then keep only the changed person, thing, or value when the repeated words are already clear.
cards.noteEn: This omission is called ellipsis: words are understood even though they are not repeated. A comma or semicolon often marks the gap. The listener recovers the missing verb and other repeated material from the first parallel part.

example.es: Ana tiene dos libros; Luis, tres.
example.en: Ana has two books; Luis has three.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something seems to have a quality or state?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of parecer followed by the describing word.
cards.noteEn: The description agrees with the person or thing: parece cansado, parece cansada, parecen cansados. This reports an impression rather than asserting the state as a fact.

cards.promptEs: debería/deberías… + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should do something?
cards.answerEn: Use an advice form of deber, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Use debería for “I,” “he,” “she,” or formal “you,” deberías for one familiar “you,” deberíamos for “we,” and deberían for a plural subject. The following action verb does not change.

cards.answerEn: to let my ... grow; marks me as the person whose appearance changes
cards.noteEn: Dejarme combines dejar with me. Before crecer plus hair or another body feature, me identifies whose appearance changes; natural English usually expresses that relationship with “my.”

example.es: Voy a dejarme crecer la barba.
example.en: I am going to grow out my beard.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone lets their hair, beard, or nails grow out?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching short marker with dejar, then crecer, then the body part.
cards.noteEn: The marker identifies the person whose appearance changes: dejarme crecer el pelo, dejarte crecer la barba, dejarse crecer las uñas. Spanish keeps the article before the body part where English normally uses a possessive.
Crecer is the unchanged dictionary form. With hair as its subject, it describes the hair becoming longer.

example.es: Voy a dejar crecer la barba.
example.en: I am going to grow out my beard.

cards.answerEn: my here; Spanish uses el because me already marks the affected owner
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses the definite article before an owned item when a short word such as me, te, or le already identifies the affected owner. English commonly uses a possessive instead.
Pelo usually refers to hair collectively and is masculine.
